text:
INT. DOT'S LUNCHEONETTE - LAWRENCEVILLE - EARLY MORNING (1965)
Rain streaks the front window. A neon sign buzzes OPEN backwards against the glass. Steam rises from the green coffee dispenser behind the counter.
DOT (50s), in a teal retro diner waitress dress and a white tie-waist apron, pours from a clear coffee pot with gold decals into a row of mismatched mugs. A white tea pot with a blue floral decal waits on a hot plate for the one regular who drinks tea.
On the counter: steel coffee, tea and sugar canisters, a clear square decanter of syrup, and a lady-shaped brass ashtray already half full. A retro pink alarm clock radio plays the farm report too loud.
At the grill, FRANKIE (20s), in a white double-breasted chef's coat and checkered chef's pants, flips eggs. His half apron is stained with grease. He pounds the bottom of a glass ketchup bottle over the hash browns.
FRANKIE: Who keeps watering down the ketchup?
DOT: Same guy who keeps watering down your jokes.
The bell over the door jingles. OFFICER BRESLIN (40s) shakes rain off his heavy police jacket and takes a stool. He slides a folded newspaper onto the counter and taps the headline.
BRESLIN: You see this? Coker Tire is closing the Etna store.
DOT: Coffee first, gossip second.
She sets down a cup. Breslin unwraps a stick of bubble gum, thinks better of it, and pockets it.
In the corner booth, two teenagers share a milkshake from the milkshake machine and feed dimes into the jukebox. One of them flips through a stack of magazines; the other keeps glancing at the pay phone on the wall, waiting for a call.
The pay phone rings. Everyone freezes.
DOT picks up the receiver, listens, and hands it across the counter to Breslin without a word.
BRESLIN (into phone): Diaz? Slow down.
He pulls a pistol from his holster to check it, clips it back, drops two bills next to his cup, and is gone before the coffee cools.
DOT wipes the counter, turns off the radio, and looks at the empty stool. Frankie sets a cigarette behind his ear and goes back to the eggs.
FRANKIE: Every Tuesday.
DOT: Every Tuesday.
She flips the neon sign to CLOSED, though it is only seven in the morning, and pours herself the last of the coffee.
INT. COUNTY MORGUE - NIGHT (1957)
Fluorescent tubes flicker over a steel autopsy slab where a young man lies covered to the chin. DR. ABEL MARSH (60s), sleeves rolled, in a short-sleeved white coroner's shirt, presses a stethoscope to the dead man's chest out of habit, then checks his wristwatch and writes down the time.
The old fridge in the corner shudders and hums. The radiator under the frosted window knocks and hisses.
DEPUTY RUTH OKAFOR (30s) waits on a red chair by the door, a two-way radio crackling on her hip.
RUTH: Sheriff wants your report tonight.
MARSH: Then the sheriff can type it.
He drags a portable typewriter onto the bench beside her and pecks out two lines. The rotary phone on the wall rings. Neither of them moves to answer it.
Marsh reaches for his bone saw, thinks better of it, and seals a sample in a specimen jar instead.
INT. HARTWELL INSURANCE - SECRETARIAL POOL - DAY (1962)
Fluorescent hum. MARGARET (40s) feeds a sheet into her gray typewriter and hammers out a letter. The black rotary phone on her desk rings. She answers, cradling the receiver against her shoulder while she counts dimes out of the green change machine for the bus home.
MR. DAVIES (60s) drops a thick reference manual on her desk.
DAVIES: Section nine. Before lunch.
MARGARET: I'll have the Pittsburgh file on your desk by five.
She jots a note in her steno notebook, then fills a paper cup at the water cooler and waits by the fax machine for the Erie office.
EXT. ALLEY BEHIND A BLOOMFIELD BAR - NIGHT
Rain. OFFICER DIAZ, in a Pittsburgh police heavy jacket and a black police baseball cap, steps around a pool of blood with her pistol drawn. Her partner snaps handcuffs on a suspect and calls it in on a walkie-talkie.
The CORONER, in a white short-sleeve coroner shirt, kneels by the body.
